cues.text: Sons of Thessalonica
Born in Thessalonica to a senatorial family, Cyril (originally named Constantine) in 827 and his elder brother Methodius in 826 both grew up in a bilingual Greek and Slavic border city.
This upbringing gave them a natural fluency in the Slavic tongue, unusual among educated Byzantines of their class.
Both set aside the secular honors their family background and education might easily have secured them, choosing instead the priesthood.
Both spent time in monastic life on the shores of the Bosphorus before the mission that would define their lives found them.
An Alphabet Invented for a Mission
The Prince of Moravia requested missionaries from Constantinople who could teach and worship in the Slavic tongue rather than Latin.
The emperor and patriarch turned to Cyril and Methodius, whose command of Slavic made them uniquely suited to the task.
Since no written form of the Slavic language yet existed, Cyril undertook the extraordinary labor of inventing one: the Glagolitic alphabet .
The later Cyrillic alphabet would eventually develop from it and is still used today across Russia and much of the Slavic world.
With this new alphabet, the brothers translated the Gospels and the essential liturgical books into Old Church Slavonic.
For the first time, the Slavic peoples of Great Moravia could hear the word of God and worship in a language they actually understood, rather than a foreign tongue learned only by the educated few.
Suspicion from Rival Missionaries
The brothers arrived in Moravia in 863 and labored there for four and a half years.
Their success provoked fierce resentment from German missionaries already established in the region.
They viewed the Slavonic liturgy as both a doctrinal irregularity and a direct threat to their own influence.
Some German churchmen insisted that only Hebrew, Greek, and Latin — the three languages inscribed above Christ's cross — were fit for sacred worship.
This position would have permanently excluded the Slavic peoples from ever hearing the liturgy in their own tongue.
Vindicated in Rome
Summoned to answer these accusations before the pope, Cyril and Methodius traveled to Rome.
There, Pope Adrian II, after careful examination, decisively vindicated their mission.
He approved the Slavonic liturgy, personally welcomed the brothers, and ordained both of them bishops.

This formal papal endorsement settled, at the highest level of Church authority, the principle they had staked their whole mission on: no people should be denied access to the Gospel and the liturgy in their own living language.
One Brother's Death, and the Other's Endurance
Cyril died in Rome on 14 February 869, only forty-two years old, entrusting to his brother the task of continuing their shared mission.
Methodius, consecrated archbishop and sent back to Moravia and Pannonia, continued the work alone for another sixteen years.
He endured fierce ongoing opposition from German churchmen, who at one point had him arrested and imprisoned for over two years.
Pope John VIII secured his release and restoration to his see.
Legacy
The Slavonic liturgy and alphabet the two brothers gave the Slavic peoples became the seedbed of an entire literary and liturgical civilization.
It stretched from the Balkans to Russia, while their pupils, scattered after Methodius's own death in 885, carried the work forward across the whole of the Slavic world.
Declared co-patrons of Europe by Pope John Paul II in 1980 alongside St. Benedict , Cyril and Methodius remain enduring witnesses to a truth the whole Church has come to treasure.
The Gospel is never more fully itself than when it learns to speak, without compromise or shortcut, in the actual living language of the people it has come to save.
Wherever the liturgy is celebrated today in a people's own mother tongue, something of these two brothers' original, hard-won conviction is still quietly at work.
